content.text: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has examined whether teacher-provided, peer-provided, and automated feedback improve accuracy, revision behaviour, and engagement. Razmi and Ghane (2024) found that an experimental group receiving direct unfocused WCF outperformed a control group on writing performance, with a large effect size (d = 1.32), and also reported higher writing self-efficacy and lower writing anxiety. The study's design, however, was limited: 52 intermediate male EFL learners aged 12–18 were assessed, and the authors acknowledged that the small, gender-restricted sample constrains generalisability (Razmi & Ghane, 2024). The study randomly assigned 139 low-intermediate EFL writers to four experimental conditions and a self-correction control group (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

The corpus was small—30 essays from intermediate Chinese undergraduates—and the authors noted that findings may not generalise to other proficiency levels or genres (Luo et al., 2025). Yet Koltovskaia (2022) found no division of labour between teachers and Grammarly, with all six participating teachers providing feedback on both higher-order and lower-order concerns despite Grammarly's availability. Zhang and Hyland (2021) reported that 88% of 33 students submitted to an AWE system more than five times (mean = 9.5 submissions), and students reported spending more time revising after AWE feedback (6.2 hours) than after peer (5.8 hours) or teacher feedback (4.7 hours).
